title: Shemini: grief has its reasons (Leviticus 10:16–20)
hook: Aaron doesn't eat the offering in his grief; Moses hears him out and agrees

segments.voice: Yesterday, Aaron's silence. Your line was and Aaron held his peace. Did you wait a breath before answering someone? Today, the same terrible day, and Aaron finally speaks. Day three hundred ninety-three.

A manager notices a missed deadline and walks over, ready to say something sharp. Then the employee says, quietly: my father died on Tuesday. And the manager has a choice. Hold the line, because rules are rules. Or hear the reason, and let it change the answer. The same afternoon Aaron lost his sons, there was still work to do in the sanctuary. One offering was supposed to be eaten by the priests. It wasn't. It was burned instead. And Moses, who has just lost two nephews himself, goes looking for it.
screen: `MY FATHER DIED ON TUESDAY.` → `RULES, OR REASONS?` → `MOSES GOES LOOKING.`

segments.voice: First, Moses searches. The Hebrew says darosh darash, he searched and searched, for the goat of the sin offering, and finds it burned. He's angry, and he aims it at Aaron's two surviving sons, Elazar and Itamar: why didn't you eat it in the holy place, as I commanded? An old scribal tradition, recorded in the Talmud, counts darosh darash as the middle words of the whole Torah. The center of the scroll is a man searching. Second, Aaron answers for his sons. He speaks for the first time since the fire. In plain words: today they brought their offerings, and today such things have happened to me. If I had eaten the sin offering today, would that have been good in God's eyes? He doesn't argue the law. He names his grief, and asks whether a mourner's meal is the kind of holiness God wants. Third, Moses hears. The text says that when Moses heard, it was good in his eyes. Rashi adds the striking part: Moses admitted it, and wasn't ashamed to say, I hadn't heard that rule. The great lawgiver, on the worst day, says: you're right, and I was wrong. Fourth, the lesson commentators draw. A law can make room for a mourner. And the person who holds authority can change course after listening, without losing anything that matters. Jewish law still does this: a mourner before the funeral is exempt from many commandments, so the grief can be what it is.
screen: `DAROSH DARASH: HE SEARCHED HARD.` · `AARON NAMES HIS GRIEF.` · `MOSES HEARS, AND IT WAS GOOD.` · `THE LAW MAKES ROOM FOR MOURNERS.` · then, large: `MOSES HEARD, AND AGREED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone grieve their own way. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you love who is carrying something heavy, and handling it differently than you would. Too quiet, too busy, too angry, too much. Notice the rule in you that says they're doing it wrong. Then, like Moses, hear their reason, even if you have to imagine it. Let it be good in your eyes. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayers just as they are. The bell holds the time.
Shemini, the eighth: the portion where Aaron, in his grief, doesn't eat the offering, and Moses listens, and agrees.
Your line: moses heard, and agreed. Today, when someone's choice puzzles you, ask for the reason before you correct it. Day three hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In Jewish law a mourner between a death and the burial, an onen, is exempt from many positive commandments, and during shiva the community brings food and leads prayers in the mourner's home so the mourner can simply grieve.

fork.setup: you're Moses. the offering that should have been eaten was burned, and Aaron says: after what happened to me today, would eating it have been good? what do you do?
options: insist the law is the law.
fork.reveal: Moses heard, and it was good in his eyes. Rashi says he wasn't ashamed to admit he'd been wrong.

original.note: Hebrew: "and it was good in his eyes": how Moses took Aaron's answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses was the strict one.
what it means: the lawgiver listened to a grieving brother and changed his mind.
what a scholar hears: Rashi says Moses wasn't ashamed to admit he hadn't heard; and darosh darash in 10:16 is counted as the middle words of the Torah (Kiddushin 30a).

sources.ref: laws of the onen (Mishnah Berakhot 3:1; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 341)

notes: Aaron's reply (10:19) and 'it was good in his eyes' (10:20) are paraphrased, not quoted.
Rashi on 10:20: 'he admitted and was not ashamed to say: I did not hear (it)'; confirm wording.
Kiddushin 30a: darosh darash as the middle of the Torah's words; confirm, and note that modern counts differ.
Onen exemptions cited from Mishnah Berakhot 3:1 and Shulchan Aruch YD 341; confirm citations.
Moses' anger is directed at Elazar and Itamar in the text (10:16); the script keeps that.
